summary: Defines a base set of syntaxes and matching rules for LDAP attributes. Syntaxes constrain how values look; matching rules tell the server how to compare values. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: Rules for what a phone number or name field may look like, and for how to tell whether two entries are the same.

questions: what is an ldap matching rule
what is the directory string syntax
subtitle: The base data types and comparison rules that every LDAP directory attribute is built from.

tldr.problem: Every attribute in an LDAP directory needs a defined format for its values, and a defined way to tell whether two values are equal, ordered or match a substring. Without shared definitions, clients and servers would not interoperate.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a base set of syntaxes, each with an object identifier and an LDAP-specific text encoding, and a base set of matching rules, each with an assertion syntax and an identifier. Syntaxes say how values look, and matching rules say how they are compared.
tldr.outcome: It replaces the syntax and matching rule parts of RFC 2252 and RFC 2256 and is part of the LDAP technical specification. Servers SHOULD recognize all the listed syntaxes and SHOULD implement most of the matching rules.

today: RFC 4517 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata for this site lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It replaced the syntax and matching rule parts of RFC 2252 and RFC 2256 and is part of the LDAP technical specification in RFC 4510.

sections.title: What This Document Defines
sections.content:
Each attribute stored in an LDAP directory has a defined syntax, which is its data type and constrains the structure and format of its values. The way values are compared is not part of the syntax. It comes from separately defined matching rules. A matching rule takes an argument called an assertion value, which has its own defined syntax.

This RFC defines a base set of both. Section 3 covers syntaxes and Section 4 covers matching rules. Readers are advised to read the directory information models in RFC 4512 first. The document is an integral part of the LDAP technical specification, RFC 4510.

It obsoletes RFC 2252 and RFC 2256 and updates RFC 3698. It also obsoletes all but Section 2.11 of RFC 3698. Some schema elements from the previous specification are not carried over. PKI schema elements moved to a separate RFC, and unless reintroduced, the remainder are to be considered Historic.
sections.eli5: Every box in the directory has a rule for what can go inside, and a separate rule for how to tell two contents apart. This document writes both sets of rules.

sections.title: Syntaxes Versus Matching Rules
sections.content:
Splitting format from comparison matters. A string like Smith and SMITH have the same syntax. Whether they count as equal depends on the matching rule the attribute uses, such as one that ignores case or one that is exact.

An attribute type definition names a syntax by its object identifier and can name matching rules for equality, ordering and substring matching. The RFC says each matching rule description states whether it suits use as EQUALITY, ORDERING or SUBSTR. The syntax of the assertion value is typically, but not necessarily, the same as the syntax of the attribute values.

A matching rule evaluates to TRUE, and in some cases Undefined, as its description states, and otherwise to FALSE.
sections.eli5: A sticker saying "words only" is the syntax. A teacher deciding whether "Cat" and "cat" count as the same word is the matching rule.

sections.title: LDAP-Specific Encoding and Object Identifiers
sections.content:
Each syntax describes how values are represented when transferred in the LDAP protocol. This is called the LDAP-specific encoding, to distinguish it from other encodings such as the BER encoding used by X.500. It always produces octet-aligned values and, where possible, character strings that clients can display with little or no translation. Clients MUST NOT assume, though, that the encoding of an unrecognized syntax is human-readable. JPEG is one example where a readable form is not reasonable.

Each syntax is identified by an object identifier in dotted-decimal form. Short names are not defined for syntaxes, and the identifiers are not meant to be shown to users. A suggested minimum upper bound on length may be added in curly braces after the identifier. For example 1.3.6.1.4.1.1466.115.121.1.15{64} suggests that values can be up to 64 characters. Because UTF-8 is variable-length, 64 characters may take more than 64 octets.
sections.eli5: Each kind of box has a long numbered label for computers to read, and a simple written form for the things inside it.

sections.title: The Defined Syntaxes
sections.content:
The syntaxes cover simple types and directory-specific ones. Among them are Boolean (TRUE or FALSE), Integer (a whole number of unlimited magnitude written as decimal digits), Bit String (such as '0101111101'B), Country String (two-character ISO 3166 codes such as US), IA5 String, Numeric String, Printable String, Octet String, OID, JPEG and Telephone Number. Others describe schema definitions, such as Attribute Type Description and Object Class Description.

Directory String is a string of one or more arbitrary characters from the Universal Character Set, encoded as UTF-8. A zero-length string is not permitted, and servers and clients MUST be prepared for arbitrary code points, including unassigned ones. Attribute types using it should not restrict the format with patterns. A new syntax should be defined in such cases.

The DN syntax is the purported distinguished name of an entry, encoded using the string form from RFC 4514, for example UID=jsmith,DC=example,DC=net. Generalized Time is a restriction of ISO 8601. The "Z" time zone form SHOULD be used in preference to a differential, and the examples 199412161032Z and 199412160532-0500 mean the same instant.
sections.eli5: There is one kind of box for yes or no, one for whole numbers, one for words, one for a name-with-address, and so on. Each kind has a plain written way to fill it in.

sections.title: The Matching Rules
sections.content:
A matching rule is applied through an assertion in an LDAP filter. Each rule states which attribute syntaxes it applies to, using conditions on the corresponding ASN.1 type, and the assertion syntax. Each also has a unique object identifier. The definition of a matching rule should not subsequently be changed. If a change is wanted, a new rule with a new identifier should be defined.

The rules are named for what they compare. Examples are caseExactMatch, caseIgnoreMatch, integerMatch, booleanMatch, distinguishedNameMatch, generalizedTimeMatch, octetStringMatch and telephoneNumberMatch, along with ordering and substring variants.

For string rules, nominated character strings are first prepared using the string preparation algorithms of RFC 4518, whose steps are Transcode, Map, Normalize, Prohibit and Check bidi, plus insignificant character handling. The two compared strings are equal if they have the same number of characters with the same code points after preparation. The exact and ignore-case rules differ in the Map step, where case is folded or not.

Some rules compare only part of a value. For example directoryStringFirstComponentMatch applies caseIgnoreMatch to the first component of a value that is a SEQUENCE.
sections.eli5: Before comparing two words, the server tidies them, and then checks them letter by letter. One rule treats big and small letters as different, and another does not.

sections.title: What Servers Must and Should Do
sections.content:
Servers SHOULD recognize all the syntaxes listed in the RFC, but are not required to otherwise support them. They MAY recognize other syntaxes, although defining additional arbitrary syntaxes is discouraged because it hinders interoperability.

For matching rules, servers MAY implement wordMatch and keywordMatch, but SHOULD implement the others. Servers that implement the extensibleMatch filter SHOULD allow the listed rules in that filter and with all known attribute types where the assertion syntax matches the value syntax. Servers MUST publish, in the matchingRules attribute, the definitions of matching rules referenced by the attributeTypes and matchingRuleUse attributes in the same subschema entry. A server that supports extensibleMatch MAY use matchingRuleUse to say which rules apply to which attribute types.

The IANA section updates the LDAP descriptors registry with the matching rule names and identifiers defined here.
sections.eli5: A server should know all the standard box types and most of the comparing rules, and it has to list the rules it is using so clients can look them up.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The LDAP-specific encodings do not define canonical encodings. Converting to another encoding such as BER and back does not necessarily reproduce the original octets. So these encodings should not be used where a canonical encoding is required. They also cannot always be reversed to the original DER, for example for Directory String and DN values, so they should not be used where reversibility to DER is needed, such as verifying digital signatures.

The RFC adds a requirement: when interpreting security-sensitive fields, especially those used to grant or deny access, implementations MUST ensure that matching rule comparisons are done on the underlying abstract value, regardless of the particular encoding used.
sections.eli5: The same thing can be written down in more than one way. When a decision about who gets in depends on it, compare what it means, not how it was written.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 2252
sections.content:
Appendix B is informational and lists differences from RFC 2252. Syntax formats are now written in ABNF, and the descriptions were expanded so they depend less on knowledge of X.500. The relationship of each syntax to its ASN.1 type is explicit.

Some syntaxes were removed or moved. The Binary syntax was removed as not adequately specified, and the PKI-related syntaxes moved to another RFC. Syntaxes that were referenced but never defined were dropped. Syntaxes from RFC 2256, such as Delivery Method, Guide and Octet String, were incorporated. The printable string character set was corrected, and Directory String, Printable String and Telephone Number values must now have at least one character. Matching rules from RFC 3698 and RFC 2798 were added and string preparation was applied to string rules.
sections.eli5: This is the list of what got fixed, added or thrown out compared with the older version.
